books.section: Great Depression and the New Deal (1929-1939)

stimulus.text: Senator Huey Long of Louisiana, photographed in 1935 seated at a desk in front of shelves of law books, gesturing with both hands as he speaks. Long built a national following with his Share Our Wealth program, which proposed capping large fortunes and guaranteeing every family a homestead and a minimum income.
stimulus.source_note: Huey Long at desk, 1935 press photograph. Public domain; via Wikimedia Commons.

source: original; stimulus photograph by an unknown press photographer, 1935, public domain
stem: Long's movement most threatened Roosevelt chiefly because it

options.text: Mobilized a mass following on the populist left
Came from the Republican right and its corporate backers
options.misconception: Long attacked concentrated wealth, so corporate backers were his targets, not his base.

options.text: Opposed all government spending on principle entirely
options.misconception: Long demanded massive government action to share wealth; opposing spending was the conservatives' position.

options.text: Demanded immediate American entry into World War II
options.misconception: Long was assassinated in 1935, years before the war, and his movement was about the Depression, not foreign policy.

rationales.A: Background from the books: with thousands of Share Our Wealth clubs and millions of followers, Long was Roosevelt's most dangerous rival, pushing him toward the Second New Deal.
rationales.B: Background from the books: Long's movement came from the populist left, not from the Republican right or from business.
rationales.C: Background from the books: Long's plan required heavy government spending and steep taxes, the opposite of opposing spending.
rationales.D: Background from the books: Long died in 1935, before the war began, and his program was about wealth at home, not war abroad.
rationales.general:
1. The passage says Long built a national following around sharing wealth.
2. The books count thousands of Share Our Wealth clubs and millions of followers.
3. That following sat to Roosevelt's left, demanding more action, not less.
4. A rival who can pull your own voters leftward is the most dangerous kind.
Remember: a threat from your own side pulls policy further than a threat from the other side.
